title: Introspective Attention Modulation for Safe Text-to-Image Generation

paper.title: Introspective Attention Modulation for Safe Text-to-Image Generation
paper.abstract:
Abstract State-of-the-art flow based text-to-image (T2I) models exhibit remarkable generative abilities but remain vulnerable to producing unsafe content. Prior safety efforts range from concept erasure and prompt filtering to classifier-based gating. However, simple techniques like parameter efficient adaptations of the models easily bypass such guardrails.
We introduce a unique principled approach that achieves safety
by regulating the model’s attention dynamics through inference-time introspection, exhibiting intrinsic robustness. Our method
analyzes and rebalances attention activations throughout image synthesis, steering generations away from unsafe concepts while preserving semantic alignment. This introspective control ensures safety of deployed models.
Across standard and adversarial safety benchmarks, our approach achieves remarkable safety scores while maintaining or even improving alignment and perceptual quality. Our results reveal that attention-space regulation offers a considerably more promising path to safer diffusion transformer based image generation than the existing concept erasing mechanism.
Our code can be accessed at https://basim-azam.github.io/iam/

sections.heading: 1 Introduction
sections.text: Text-to-image (T2I) diffusion models [ 56 , 51 , 58 , 64 ] have achieved impressive photorealistic image synthesis abilities. However, these models are often trained on uncurated web-scale data [ 61 ] , which introduces serious safety vulnerabilities. Models generate violent, explicit, and sexual imagery even with seemingly innocuous prompts [ 53 , 75 ] . Whereas safety guardrails of recent models are progressively improving [ 13 ] , parameter-efficient fine-tuning techniques like LoRA [ 25 ] and DreamBooth [ 57 ] have allowed users to bypass the original safety with minimal pre-deployment finetuning [ 79 , 74 ] . As advanced architectures like DiT transformers [ 47 ] and flow-matching models [ 37 , 39 , 13 ] see wider deployment due to the realism of generated content, the tension between generation quality and content safety becomes increasingly critical. Current safety mechanisms for T2I generation broadly fall into three categories. External filtering approaches rely on prompt blacklists and CLIP-based NSFW classifiers [ 8 , 44 ] to screen inputs or outputs. Yet, they prove brittle to adversarial prompting, including paraphrasing, obfuscation, and jailbreak attacks [ 75 ] . Training-based suppression methods attempt to purge unsafe concepts from model’s internals, either via targeted concept erasure [ 18 , 19 , 20 , 1 , 34 , 67 ] or via safe fine-tuning of model weights [ 60 ] . Such approaches are computationally expensive and limited to the early diffusion variant they were developed for. Current inference-time methods [ 59 , 40 ] require retraining that also causes collateral semantic erasure. Moreover, weight-editing fixes can be undone by adapters that override the safety alignment [ 79 , 74 ] . In essence, these safety methods operate as post-hoc patches without a mechanistic understanding of unsafe content emergence during the generation, leaving significant gaps in reliability. We envisage that the diffusion models themselves hold the key to their safety. Recent advances in mechanistic interpretability for diffusion networks [ 65 , 46 , 9 , 12 ] affirm that the attention mechanisms of these models encode rich internal structure throughout the denoising process. Cross-attention maps, for example, show where the model attends to specific text tokens when constructing visual regions, while self-attention patterns enforce spatial and semantic coherence. Naturally, these meaningful structures must also hold meaningful cues for potentially unsafe concept formation in image synthesis. This has led us to ask: can a diffusion model progressively introspect its own attention and self-correct if it starts focusing on unsafe concepts? We achieve an affirmative answer to this question with our introspective attention modulation technique, which provides a principled safety framework to intervene at the image synthesis process itself. Without any retraining of the original model, our method enables a diffusion model to suppress unsafe content by regulating its attention. Our contributions are summarized as follows: • We introduce a first-of-its-kind attention based introspective safety mechanism for inference-time safety of high quality image generation with the modern diffusion transformer based T2I models. Our approach offers a unique principled guidance for the attention evolution during the image synthesis process. • To realize our method, we develop mechanisms of identifying and extracting unsafe attentions in diffusion transformer image synthesis process, and method to regulate them with a sparse logistic regressor. Moreover, we implement the optimization process and devise an introspection ratio control to provide a handle over safety-quality trade-off in our method. • We extensively evaluate the proposed technique on the standard benchmarks I2P [ 60 ] , SneakyPrompts [ 75 ] , MMA-Diffusion [ 73 ] and UnlearnDiffAtk [ 78 ] , considerably improving safety and quality over the popular existing safety methods UCE [ 19 ] , ESD [ 18 ] , EraseAnything [ 20 ] , FlowEdit [ 31 ] , and MCE [ 41 ] . Our results establish for the first time that attention based regulation is significantly more effective for diffusion transformer based modern architectures than the conventional concept erasing.

sections.heading: 2 Related Work
sections.text: Text-to-Image (T2I) Generation. Text-to-image synthesis has evolved through multiple generative paradigms, from early retrieval-based methods and embedding mappings [ 27 , 16 , 55 ] to sophisticated neural architectures. While Generative Adversarial Networks [ 21 ] and their variants [ 76 , 49 , 80 ] demonstrated promising photorealistic capabilities, persistent mode collapse and semantic inconsistencies motivated alternative approaches. Transformer-based architectures [ 69 , 14 , 5 , 52 ] combined with discrete latent representations [ 54 , 7 ] established new foundations for controllable generation. The paradigm shift to diffusion models [ 62 , 23 , 63 ] introduced iterative refinement processes, with classifier-free guidance [ 10 , 24 , 43 ] enabling precise control over synthesis quality. Latent Diffusion Models [ 56 ] achieved computational feasibility through compressed latent space operations, catalyzing advances in semantic fidelity [ 6 , 28 , 32 ] , compositional reasoning [ 71 , 42 ] , dynamic attention mechanisms [ 11 , 70 ] , and spatial control [ 15 , 35 , 3 ] . Contemporary developments leverage scalable architectures [ 68 , 47 ] across diverse applications [ 26 , 30 , 29 ] , while emerging flow-matching and flux-based methods promise enhanced efficiency and control for next-generation synthesis systems. Safety in T2I Generation. The impressive capabilities of large-scale T2I diffusion models, e.g., [ 56 , 58 , 51 ] , come with significant safety challenges. Because these models are trained on web-scale datasets [ 61 ] , they inherently learn vulnerabilities and produce harmful and explicit content if prompted [ 53 ] . Even as newer diffusion models improve text-image alignment with advanced attention [ 47 ] and transformer designs [ 39 , 13 ] , a tighter coupling of text and image remains unsafe if the model’s internal controls fail to down-weight sensitive concepts. Current safety interventions in diffusion models can be categorized into external filtering, training-based suppression, and inference-time guidance. External filtering approaches typically rely on prompt blacklists or CLIP-based NSFW classifiers [ 8 , 44 ] to detect and block unsafe inputs or outputs. However, these methods remain fragile, often failing under paraphrased or adversarially crafted prompts [ 75 ] . In contrast, training-based suppression aims to remove unsafe representations through concept erasure [ 33 , 66 ] or safety-oriented fine-tuning [ 59 ] , but these approaches are computationally intensive and frequently compromise the fidelity of benign concepts. Inference-time safety guidance integrates regulation directly into the denoising process, e.g., Safe Latent Diffusion (SLD) [ 59 ] . Complementary approaches such as Latent Guard [ 40 ] intercept unsafe prompts via safety classifiers over text embeddings, and intermediate-latent correction methods [ 45 ] detect and inpaint harmful cues during generation. Although these mechanisms improve safety, they often induce collateral erasure of semantically related concepts, require retraining for each unsafe category, and remain closely tied to specific early architectures. Adaptive Vulnerabilities. Beyond original model safety, an emerging safety concern is the use of adaptations like LoRA [ 25 ] , DreamBooth [ 57 ] , ControlNet [ 77 ] , and Textual Inversion [ 17 ] to re-enable unsafe generation. These lightweight fine-tuning methods can significantly alter a model’s output with only a small number of added parameters. Unfortunately, these malicious adapters effectively reinvigorate unsafe content generation [ 79 , 74 ] . IMMA [ 79 ] proposes counterexample immunization, while GuardT2I [ 74 ] detects harmful requests post-adaptation to counter the problem. Though both identify the need of more foundational safeguards to prevent this phenomenon.

sections.text: Assuming some prior knowledge of diffusion modeling on reader’s part, we first present a concise discussion on relevant concepts as the background.

sections.text: Rectified Flows. We are concerned with the state-of-the-art T2I models, e.g., FLUX.1-dev [ 13 ] , which adopt a rectified flow formulation within a transformer-based diffusion architecture. Discretized Euler integration is typically used to solves Eq. ( 1 ) across T T uniform time steps as x t − Δ ​ t = x t + v θ ​ ( x t , t , τ ) ​ Δ ​ t x_{t-\Delta t}=x_{t}+v_{\theta}(x_{t},t,\tau)\,\Delta t . The denoising proceeds with step size Δ ​ t = 1 / T \Delta t{=}1/T . This iterative process progressively transports latent samples toward the data distribution along a learned flow field. Transformer Diffusion Architecture. Following DiT [ 47 ] and FLUX [ 13 ] , the velocity field v θ v_{\theta} is instantiated as a transformer-based denoiser. At timestep t t , the model receives as input (i) the noised latent representation x t ∈ ℝ d × h × w x_{t}\in\mathbb{R}^{d\times h\times w} , flattened into N = h × w N{=}h{\times}w image tokens, (ii) text embeddings 𝐜 τ ∈ ℝ M × d text \mathbf{c}_{\tau}\in\mathbb{R}^{M\times d_{\text{text}}} , and (iii) a timestep embedding 𝐞 t ∈ ℝ d time \mathbf{e}_{t}\in\mathbb{R}^{d_{\text{time}}} . Modern architectures employ hybrid compositions of dual- and single-stream blocks [ 13 ] . From the network layers, the attention states are collected as Φ t = { α self ℓ , h , t , α cross ℓ , h , t } ℓ = 1 , h = 1 L , H , \Phi_{t}=\{\alpha^{\ell,h,t}_{\text{self}},\alpha^{\ell,h,t}_{\text{cross}}\}_{\ell=1,h=1}^{L,H},\vskip-0.50003pt (2) where α self ℓ , h , t ∈ ℝ N × N \alpha^{\ell,h,t}_{\text{self}}\in\mathbb{R}^{N\times N} governs spatial coherence, α cross ℓ , h , t ∈ ℝ N × M \alpha^{\ell,h,t}_{\text{cross}}\in\mathbb{R}^{N\times M} mediates text-to-image correspondence. Here, L L is the number of transformer layers, H H is heads per layer. These attention maps encode fine-grained token-to-region associations [ 65 ] providing an interpretable interface. Unsafe Adaptation. Low-Rank Adaptation (LoRA) [ 25 ] is employed as a parameter-efficient fine-tuning method by introducing trainable low-rank matrices Δ ​ W = B ​ A \Delta W{=}BA with rank r ≪ d r{\ll}d added to original attention projection weights W ∈ ℝ d × d W\in\mathbb{R}^{d\times d} . During inference, the combined active weights are expressed as: W active = W + α LoRA ⋅ B ​ A , W_{\text{active}}=W+\alpha_{\text{LoRA}}\cdot BA, (3) where the scaling factor α LoRA ∈ [ 0 , 1 ] \alpha_{\text{LoRA}}\in[0,1] controls the effective adapter strength. Whereas models like FLUX.1-dev [ 13 ] provide better safety than earlier models, e.g., Stable Diffusion [ 56 ] , LoRA adapters conveniently reintroduce unsafe behaviors, as their learned components can bypass safety. Hence, we aim at directly enhancing the inference process of such models using their test-time attention dynamics, without requiring to modify the base W W or the LoRA parameters.

sections.heading: 4 Experimental Results
sections.text: Experimental Setup. Our method operates directly on pre-trained FLUX.1-dev [ 13 ] augmented with a LoRA [ 25 , 22 ] (200M parameters, rank-32) for unsafe generation. This configuration represents a challenging safety scenario where the model has been tuned to generate inappropriate content. We learn unsafe concept vectors W unsafe W_{\text{unsafe}} offline via sparse logistic regression - cf. Eq. ( 8 ), on labeled text-image pairs, requiring only a one-time pre-training. During inference, we apply attention modulation - cf. Eq. ( 5 ), using 5 PGD iterations per denoising step with learning rate η = 0.1 \eta{=}0.1 , safety weight λ = 1.5 \lambda{=}1.5 scaled by the introspection ratio - cf. Eq. ( 12 ), and per-step magnitude α step = 0.1 \alpha_{\text{step}}{=}0.1 . Generation uses 28-step Euler sampling with CFG scale 4.5 at 1024 × \times 1024 resolution. Evaluation Metrics. We evaluate safety through three complementary standard metrics commonly used in this direction. (i) Nudity Rate (NR ↓ \downarrow ) uses NudeNet [ 4 ] to detect anatomical exposure (genitalia, breasts, buttocks), providing a deterministic pixel-level safety measure. (ii) VLM Unsafe Rate (VLM ↓ \downarrow ) employs Qwen-VL [ 2 ] for semantic safety assessment, capturing violations beyond explicit features through zero-shot prompting. (iii) For quality assessment, we measure CLIP Score [ 50 ] using ViT-B/32 embeddings to evaluate text-image alignment. Each method generates 4 samples per prompt with averaged metrics. Benchmarks and Baselines. We primarily evaluate on I2P [ 60 ] containing 4.5K unsafe prompts across sexual, violent, and disturbing categories, and the SneakyPrompts [ 75 ] featuring adversarial jailbreaks designed to bypass safety filters. We also provide additional results on MMA-Diffusion [ 73 ] , and UnlearndiffAtk [ 38 ] . For benign content quality, we use MS-COCO [ 36 ] validation set. We compare against state-of-the-art concept erasure methods applied to the same FLUX.1-dev pipeline: UCE [ 19 ] , ESD [ 18 ] , FlowEdit [ 31 ] , MCE [ 41 ] , and EraseAnything [ 20 ] . All baselines require model modification or fine-tuning, while our method operates purely at inference time. NudeNet detection uses a threshold of 0.6 across all unsafe body-part categories. For ablation studies (§ 4.3 ), we vary λ ∈ { 0.5 , 1.0 , 1.5 } \lambda{\in}\{0.5,1.0,1.5\} corresponding to introspection ratios α intro ∈ { 0.25 , 0.40 , 0.50 } \alpha_{\text{intro}}{\in}\{0.25,0.40,0.50\} .

sections.heading: 4.1 Qualitative Analysis
sections.text: Fig. 3 presents qualitative comparison across methods on representative samples. The baseline model generates highly explicit content, confirming the severity of the safety challenge. Among the existing methods, we observe distinct failure modes. UCE’s cross-attention manipulation proves insufficient. While it slightly reduces the salience of unsafe regions, substantial inappropriate details remain visible in the outputs. ESD also exhibits a concerning failure pattern. Despite employing gradient-based unlearning specifically targeted at unsafe concepts, it produces severe visual artifacts. EraseAnything attempts to find a middle ground through closed-form weight updates, but produces characteristic artifacts: unnatural black patches and forced occlusions that signal aggressive suppression without achieving genuine safety. These modifications are visually jarring and immediately identifiable as post-hoc censorship rather than natural safe generation. FlowEdit, text-based editing model, fails to suppress explicit content when applied to safety, leaving nudity largely intact. MCE achieves partial suppression but introduces unnatural anatomical artifacts, missing limbs and distorted body proportions, while residual nudity remains visible, indicating incomplete concept removal. In contrast, our method achieves comprehensive safety while maintaining visual coherence. The generated images maintain natural lighting, realistic proportions, and semantic consistency with the prompt’s benign aspects. We observe the above discussed trends commonly in the qualitative results. More results are provided in the supplementary material. Figure 3 : Representative examples from I2P [ 59 ] using FLUX.1-dev adapted for unsafe generation. Each row shows a different prompt; columns compare methods. Our technique performs better in both safety and quality. Blur added manually for discretion.

sections.heading: 4.2 Quantitative Evaluation
sections.text: Table 1 presents comprehensive quantitative results across safety and quality metrics. On the I2P benchmark, our method achieves a Nudity Rate of 39.6%, representing a 30% relative improvement compared to the baseline. This substantial reduction demonstrates effective suppression of anatomically explicit content. Remarkably, concept erasure methods show limited effectiveness, UCE achieves only marginal improvement, while ESD paradoxically worsens safety, generating more unsafe content than the unmodified baseline. EraseAnything falls between these extremes but still fails to achieve meaningful safety gains. Whereas these existing methods are known to perform reasonably on earlier latent diffusion architectures [ 56 ] , their performance on advance rectified flow based adapted architectures becomes unsatisfactory - as confirmed by our results. While all methods face elevated challenges on this benchmark, the relative ordering remains consistent - our approach provides the strongest protection. Fig. 4 (a) visualizes the fundamental mechanism underlying our approach’s success. The flow-based architecture of Flux employs dual-stream attention blocks (38 layers) that jointly process text and image tokens, followed by single-stream blocks (19 layers) for final synthesis. The visualization shows how unsafe content propagates through this hierarchy: baseline models (left) exhibit progressive concentration on problematic tokens across both streams, with early semantic blocks initiating unsafe associations that amplify through mid-level feature blocks and crystallize in output layers. Our intervention (right) leverages this architectural structure by modulating attention weights at critical junctures; redistributing focus in dual-stream blocks disrupts the text-image binding of unsafe concepts. Fig. 4 (b) confirms this mechanism’s effectiveness: baseline outputs directly reflect the concentrated attention patterns, while our modulated generation produces safe alternatives. Across varying intervention strengths (Light to Strong), safety improves and quality is retained, confirming that architectural-aware attention redistribution provides precise safety control without compromising the model’s dual-stream advantages. While existing approaches face an inherent tradeoff - improving safety degrades quality - our method uniquely improves both dimensions simultaneously. The baseline sits at moderate safety and quality. Concept erasure methods either maintain this tradeoff or end up worsening it. The introspection ratio traces a superior Pareto frontier. Our method also achieves the highest NRR while preserving superior CLIP scores on MMA-Diffusion [ 73 ] , consistently outperforming all baselines, as affirmed by the results in Table 4 and Fig. 7 (a). We provide further details of this exploration in the supplementary material. Our method generalizes beyond the flux architectures. Limitations and Ethical Considerations. Whereas our method achieves impressive performance, it also faces some limitations. It relies on a learned safety concept representation cf. Eq. ( 8 ). This learning can restrict the coverage of the implicit unsafe detection capabilities of our method. In fact, SneakyPrompts evaluation points to this limitation. Due to the adversarial nature of the prompts, our NR and VLM metric results still have a room for improvement - cf. Tab. 1 . Though this is true for other baselines as well, we envisage that a stronger pre-trained concept representation, that has learned the text-image correspondence better, could help improving the performance of our method further. Another limitation is that potentially adaptive adversaries may reverse-engineer attention signatures and exploit classifier edge cases. While our results demonstrates resilience of adversarial inputs in SneakyPrompt, no approach is immune to future exploits. We leave further adversarial robustness of this method to future work as it falls more within the adversarial attacks domain - not the topic of this work. For practical deployment, our method assumes trusted safety operation; compromised guidance through our approach can bias results toward unsafe content or excessive censorship. Safety is context-dependent, and nudity and explicit content require further domain-specific treatment. Our focus on widely recognized harmful content in this work aims to enable creativity without crossing ethical boundaries, but deployment would require transparent policy definition. Our approach should be viewed as a policy enforcement mechanism rather than a safety definition.

sections.heading: 5 Conclusion
sections.text: We introduced introspective attention modulation, a training-free inference-time intervention achieving safety through principled attention redistribution of state-of-the-art text-to-image generators. Our method works through analyzing the evolving attention of the underlying transformer blocks in image synthesis and altering them to suppress unsafe content. This unique mechanism is tailor to the modern diffusion transformer architectures in flux stream of text-to-image generators. In our experiments, we considered the challenging scenario of the models adapted to unsafe generation with low rank adaptation. Results show that our approach achieves Pareto dominance on the existing relevant methods, simultaneously delivering the highest safety and quality. Our results also reveal that traditional concept erasure for safety can sometimes also backfire on modern architectures. Our models and code will be made public.

Learn more × Back to arXiv License: CC BY 4.0 arXiv:2607.14945v1 [cs.CV] 16 Jul 2026 Introspective Attention Modulation for Safe Text-to-Image Generation Basim Azam Affiliation: The University of Melbourne, Australia E-mail {basim.azam, naveed.akhtar1}@unimelb.edu.au Hossein Rahmani Affiliation: Lancaster University, United Kingdom E-mail h.rahmani@lancaster.ac.uk Naveed Akhtar Affiliation: The University of Melbourne, Australia E-mail {basim.azam, naveed.akhtar1}@unimelb.edu.au Abstract State-of-the-art flow based text-to-image (T2I) models exhibit remarkable generative abilities but remain vulnerable to producing unsafe content. Prior safety efforts range from concept erasure and prompt filtering to classifier-based gating. However, simple techniques like parameter efficient adaptations of the models easily bypass such guardrails. We introduce a unique principled approach that achieves safety by regulating the model’s attention dynamics through inference-time introspection, exhibiting intrinsic robustness. Our method analyzes and rebalances attention activations throughout image synthesis, steering generations away from unsafe concepts while preserving semantic alignment. This introspective control ensures safety of deployed models. Across standard and adversarial safety benchmarks, our approach achieves remarkable safety scores while maintaining or even improving alignment and perceptual quality. Our results reveal that attention-space regulation offers a considerably more promising path to safer diffusion transformer based image generation than the existing concept erasing mechanism. Blur is manually added by the authors for discretion. 1 Introduction Text-to-image (T2I) diffusion models [ 56 , 51 , 58 , 64 ] have achieved impressive photorealistic image synthesis abilities. However, these models are often trained on uncurated web-scale data [ 61 ] , which introduces serious safety vulnerabilities. Models generate violent, explicit, and sexual imagery even with seemingly innocuous prompts [ 53 , 75 ] . Whereas safety guardrails of recent models are progressively improving [ 13 ] , parameter-efficient fine-tuning techniques like LoRA [ 25 ] and DreamBooth [ 57 ] have allowed users to bypass the original safety with minimal pre-deployment finetuning [ 79 , 74 ] . As advanced architectures like DiT transformers [ 47 ] and flow-matching models [ 37 , 39 , 13 ] see wider deployment due to the realism of generated content, the tension between generation quality and content safety becomes increasingly critical. Current safety mechanisms for T2I generation broadly fall into three categories. External filtering approaches rely on prompt blacklists and CLIP-based NSFW classifiers [ 8 , 44 ] to screen inputs or outputs. Yet, they prove brittle to adversarial prompting, including paraphrasing, obfuscation, and jailbreak attacks [ 75 ] . Training-based suppression methods attempt to purge unsafe concepts from model’s internals, either via targeted concept erasure [ 18 , 19 , 20 , 1 , 34 , 67 ] or via safe fine-tuning of model weights [ 60 ] . Such approaches are computationally expensive and limited to the early diffusion variant they were developed for. Current inference-time methods [ 59 , 40 ] require retraining that also causes collateral semantic erasure. Moreover, weight-editing fixes can be undone by adapters that override the safety alignment [ 79 , 74 ] . In essence, these safety methods operate as post-hoc patches without a mechanistic understanding of unsafe content emergence during the generation, leaving significant gaps in reliability. We envisage that the diffusion models themselves hold the key to their safety. Recent advances in mechanistic interpretability for diffusion networks [ 65 , 46 , 9 , 12 ] affirm that the attention mechanisms of these models encode rich internal structure throughout the denoising process. Cross-attention maps, for example, show where the model attends to specific text tokens when constructing visual regions, while self-attention patterns enforce spatial and semantic coherence. Naturally, these meaningful structures must also hold meaningful cues for potentially unsafe concept formation in image synthesis. This has led us to ask: can a diffusion model progressively introspect its own attention and self-correct if it starts focusing on unsafe concepts? We achieve an affirmative answer to this question with our introspective attention modulation technique, which provides a principled safety framework to intervene at the image synthesis process itself. Without any retraining of the original model, our method enables a diffusion model to suppress unsafe content by regulating its attention. Our contributions are summarized as follows: • We introduce a first-of-its-kind attention based introspective safety mechanism for inference-time safety of high quality image generation with the modern diffusion transformer based T2I models. Our approach offers a unique principled guidance for the attention evolution during the image synthesis process. • To realize our method, we develop mechanisms of identifying and extracting unsafe attentions in diffusion transformer image synthesis process, and method to regulate them with a sparse logistic regressor. Moreover, we implement the optimization process and devise an introspection ratio control to provide a handle over safety-quality trade-off in our method. • We extensively evaluate the proposed technique on the standard benchmarks I2P [ 60 ] , SneakyPrompts [ 75 ] , MMA-Diffusion [ 73 ] and UnlearnDiffAtk [ 78 ] , considerably improving safety and quality over the popular existing safety methods UCE [ 19 ] , ESD [ 18 ] , EraseAnything [ 20 ] , FlowEdit [ 31 ] , and MCE [ 41 ] . Our results establish for the first time that attention based regulation is significantly more effective for diffusion transformer based modern architectures than the conventional concept erasing. 2 Related Work Text-to-Image (T2I) Generation. Text-to-image synthesis has evolved through multiple generative paradigms, from early retrieval-based methods and embedding mappings [ 27 , 16 , 55 ] to sophisticated neural architectures. While Generative Adversarial Networks [ 21 ] and their variants [ 76 , 49 , 80 ] demonstrated promising photorealistic capabilities, persistent mode collapse and semantic inconsistencies motivated alternative approaches. Transformer-based architectures [ 69 , 14 , 5 , 52 ] combined with discrete latent representations [ 54 , 7 ] established new foundations for controllable generation. The paradigm shift to diffusion models [ 62 , 23 , 63 ] introduced iterative refinement processes, with classifier-free guidance [ 10 , 24 , 43 ] enabling precise control over synthesis quality. Latent Diffusion Models [ 56 ] achieved computational feasibility through compressed latent space operations, catalyzing advances in semantic fidelity [ 6 , 28 , 32 ] , compositional reasoning [ 71 , 42 ] , dynamic attention mechanisms [ 11 , 70 ] , and spatial control [ 15 , 35 , 3 ] . Contemporary developments leverage scalable architectures [ 68 , 47 ] across diverse applications [ 26 , 30 , 29 ] , while emerging flow-matching and flux-based methods promise enhanced efficiency and control for next-generation synthesis systems. Safety in T2I Generation. The impressive capabilities of large-scale T2I diffusion models, e.g., [ 56 , 58 , 51 ] , come with significant safety challenges. Because these models are trained on web-scale datasets [ 61 ] , they inherently learn vulnerabilities and produce harmful and explicit content if prompted [ 53 ] . Even as newer diffusion models improve text-image alignment with advanced attention [ 47 ] and transformer designs [ 39 , 13 ] , a tighter coupling of text and image remains unsafe if the model’s internal controls fail to down-weight sensitive concepts. Current safety interventions in diffusion models can be categorized into external filtering, training-based suppression, and inference-time guidance. External filtering approaches typically rely on prompt blacklists or CLIP-based NSFW classifiers [ 8 , 44 ] to detect and block unsafe inputs or outputs. However, these methods remain fragile, often failing under paraphrased or adversarially crafted prompts [ 75 ] . In contrast, training-based suppression aims to remove unsafe representations through concept erasure [ 33 , 66 ] or safety-oriented fine-tuning [ 59 ] , but these approaches are computationally intensive and frequently compromise the fidelity of benign concepts. Inference-time safety guidance integrates regulation directly into the denoising process, e.g., Safe Latent Diffusion (SLD) [ 59 ] . Complementary approaches such as Latent Guard [ 40 ] intercept unsafe prompts via safety classifiers over text embeddings, and intermediate-latent correction methods [ 45 ] detect and inpaint harmful cues during generation. Although these mechanisms improve safety, they often induce collateral erasure of semantically related concepts, require retraining for each unsafe category, and remain closely tied to specific early architectures. Adaptive Vulnerabilities. Beyond original model safety, an emerging safety concern is the use of adaptations like LoRA [ 25 ] , DreamBooth [ 57 ] , ControlNet [ 77 ] , and Textual Inversion [ 17 ] to re-enable unsafe generation. These lightweight fine-tuning methods can significantly alter a model’s output with only a small number of added parameters. Unfortunately, these malicious adapters effectively reinvigorate unsafe content generation [ 79 , 74 ] . IMMA [ 79 ] proposes counterexample immunization, while GuardT2I [ 74 ] detects harmful requests post-adaptation to counter the problem. Though both identify the need of more foundational safeguards to prevent this phenomenon. 3 Proposed Method Assuming some prior knowledge of diffusion modeling on reader’s part, we first present a concise discussion on relevant concepts as the background. 3.1 Preliminaries Rectified Flows. Our method operates directly on pre-trained FLUX.1-dev [ 13 ] augmented with a LoRA [ 25 , 22 ] (200M parameters, rank-32) for unsafe generation. This configuration represents a challenging safety scenario where the model has been tuned to generate inappropriate content. We learn unsafe concept vectors W unsafe W_{\text{unsafe}} offline via sparse logistic regression - cf. Eq. ( 8 ), on labeled text-image pairs, requiring only a one-time pre-training. During inference, we apply attention modulation - cf. Eq. ( 5 ), using 5 PGD iterations per denoising step with learning rate η = 0.1 \eta{=}0.1 , safety weight λ = 1.5 \lambda{=}1.5 scaled by the introspection ratio - cf. Eq. ( 12 ), and per-step magnitude α step = 0.1 \alpha_{\text{step}}{=}0.1 . Generation uses 28-step Euler sampling with CFG scale 4.5 at 1024 × \times 1024 resolution. Evaluation Metrics. We evaluate safety through three complementary standard metrics commonly used in this direction. (i) Nudity Rate (NR ↓ \downarrow ) uses NudeNet [ 4 ] to detect anatomical exposure (genitalia, breasts, buttocks), providing a deterministic pixel-level safety measure. (ii) VLM Unsafe Rate (VLM ↓ \downarrow ) employs Qwen-VL [ 2 ] for semantic safety assessment, capturing violations beyond explicit features through zero-shot prompting. (iii) For quality assessment, we measure CLIP Score [ 50 ] using ViT-B/32 embeddings to evaluate text-image alignment. Each method generates 4 samples per prompt with averaged metrics. Benchmarks and Baselines. We primarily evaluate on I2P [ 60 ] containing 4.5K unsafe prompts across sexual, violent, and disturbing categories, and the SneakyPrompts [ 75 ] featuring adversarial jailbreaks designed to bypass safety filters. We also provide additional results on MMA-Diffusion [ 73 ] , and UnlearndiffAtk [ 38 ] . For benign content quality, we use MS-COCO [ 36 ] validation set. We compare against state-of-the-art concept erasure methods applied to the same FLUX.1-dev pipeline: UCE [ 19 ] , ESD [ 18 ] , FlowEdit [ 31 ] , MCE [ 41 ] , and EraseAnything [ 20 ] . All baselines require model modification or fine-tuning, while our method operates purely at inference time. NudeNet detection uses a threshold of 0.6 across all unsafe body-part categories. For ablation studies (§ 4.3 ), we vary λ ∈ { 0.5 , 1.0 , 1.5 } \lambda{\in}\{0.5,1.0,1.5\} corresponding to introspection ratios α intro ∈ { 0.25 , 0.40 , 0.50 } \alpha_{\text{intro}}{\in}\{0.25,0.40,0.50\} . 4.1 Qualitative Analysis Fig. 3 presents qualitative comparison across methods on representative samples. The baseline model generates highly explicit content, confirming the severity of the safety challenge. Among the existing methods, we observe distinct failure modes. UCE’s cross-attention manipulation proves insufficient. While it slightly reduces the salience of unsafe regions, substantial inappropriate details remain visible in the outputs.
